content:
This revision is going to be fairly long, for today we are going to give you a panoramic view of the two principal moods of the Latin conjugation: the *indicative* and the *subjunctive*. But rest assured, it is only a matter of revising forms that you have already seen — apart from a few novelties that it will be useful to note in passing — and not of a lesson. In any case, if you think the dose is too strong, don't take it all in one go, but come back to it when you feel like it.

## 1. The active conjugation

### 1° The series of the present

The series of the present (in Latin one says the *infectum*, that is *the unfinished*) comprises three tenses: the PRESENT (*praesens*), the PAST (*praeteritum*) and the FUTURE (*futurum*). We should now know all three, but it may not be useless to look at them again:

**a) The present** (present of the infectum):

| | Indicative | Subjunctive |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | manduc**o**, *I eat*, manduc**as**, etc. | manduc**em**, *that I eat*, manduc**es**, etc. |
| 2nd | exerc**eo**, *I exercise*, exerc**es**, etc. | exerc**eam**, exerc**eas**, etc. |
| 3rd | ag**o**, *I do, I push*, ag**is**, ag**it**, etc., ag**unt** | ag**am**, ag**as**, etc. |
| 3rd mixed | rap**io**, *I take, I snatch*, rap**is**… rap**iunt** | rap**iam**, rap**ias**, etc. |
| 4th | fin**io**, *I finish*, fin**is**… fin**iunt** | fin**iam**, fin**ias**, etc. |

**b) The imperfect** (past of the infectum) is conjugated in the same way for the five conjugations:

| Indicative | Subjunctive |
|---|---|
| manduc**abam**, -bas, etc., *I was eating* | manduc**arem**, manduc**ares**, etc., *that I ate* |
| exerc**ebam**, ag**ebam**, rap**iebam**, fin**iebam** | exerc**erem**, ag**erem**, rap**erem**, fin**irem** |

**c) The future** (future of the infectum) exists only in the indicative, and it is generally the present subjunctive that takes the place of the future subjunctive (the same is true in French):

- 1st and 2nd conjugation, future in -bo, -bis, -bit, -bimus, -bitis, -bunt: manduc**abo**, *I will eat*, exerc**ebo**, *I will exercise*.
- For the other conjugations, future in -am, -es, -et, etc.: ag**am**, rap**iam**, fin**iam**.

We have already drawn your attention to the differences that exist between the forms of the present subjunctive and those of the future indicative (R. and N. 42). These are, moreover, as we have said, the only difficulties of the regular Latin conjugation: now that you know them better, you see that they are not very nasty. Finally, you will once again find all this in the grammatical appendix, in the form of tables easy to consult. We think that these repetitions in different forms are necessary, for to know a word or a rule well, it is the same as for knowing an object well: you have to have seen it several times, from different angles, and to have grasped or used it in different circumstances.

### 2° The series of the perfect

Let us now look at the series of the perfect or *perfectum* (*finished*).

It is very simple: it again comprises the same tenses as the series of the infectum, that is PRESENT, PAST and FUTURE. But this time, it is a question of completely finished actions, as indicated by the word *perfectum*, which is, as you must remember, the perfect (passive) participle of the verb perficere (*to do completely, to finish*).

**a) The perfect**, which we have already seen, is nothing other than the PRESENT of the perfectum. It serves first of all to express an action finished at the moment one is speaking. E.g.: vixit, perfect of vivere, *to live*, means: *he has finished living*, in other words: *he is dead*. But it can have other uses, which you will learn through usage (and which you will find in the grammatical appendix).

You must know that the form of the first person of the perfect is given in the dictionary: indeed it is enough to know it to be able to form the other tenses of the series of the perfect.

We remind you of the somewhat peculiar conjugation of the perfect indicative:

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | manducav**i**, *I have finished eating* | manducav**imus** |
| 2. | manducav**isti** | manducav**istis** |
| 3. | manducav**it** | manducav**erunt** (or sometimes manducav**ere**) |

We will likewise have: exercu**i**, eg**i**, rapu**i** and finiv**i** (or fini**i**).

Note once again that the perfect of the 1st conjugation is not always in -avi (e.g. dare gives dedi), that that of the 2nd is not always in -ui, and that those of the other conjugations are even richer in irregularities.

To obtain the *perfect subjunctive*, the endings -i, -isti, etc., are replaced by the endings -erim, -eris, etc.:

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | manducav**erim**, *that I have finished eating* | manducav**erimus** |
| 2. | manducav**eris** | manducav**eritis** |
| 3. | manducav**erit** | manducav**erint** |

Likewise: exercu**erim**, eg**erim**, rapu**erim**, finiv**erim** (or fini**erim**).

**b) The pluperfect**, or PAST of the perfectum, indicates that an action is finished at a given moment in the past; it is to the perfect what the imperfect is to the present.

To obtain the *pluperfect indicative*, one proceeds as above, but with the endings -eram, -eras, etc.:

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | manducav**eram**, *I had finished eating* | manducav**eramus** |
| 2. | manducav**eras** | manducav**eratis** |
| 3. | manducav**erat** | manducav**erant** |

Likewise: eg**eram**, exercu**eram**, rapu**eram**, finiv**eram** (or fini**eram**).

To obtain the *pluperfect subjunctive*, the endings -issem, -isses, etc. are used:

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | manducav**issem**, *that I had finished eating* | manducav**issemus** |
| 2. | manducav**isses** | manducav**issetis** |
| 3. | manducav**isset** | manducav**issent** |

Likewise: exercu**issem**, eg**issem**, rapu**issem**, finiv**issem** (or fini**issem**).

**c) The future perfect** or FUTURE of the perfectum indicates that an action will be finished at a given moment in the future. This tense exists only in the indicative; in the subjunctive, it is normally replaced by the perfect subjunctive (same principle as for the infectum: the future is replaced by the present).

The future perfect (of the indicative) is obtained by adding to the stem of the perfect the endings -ero, -eris, etc., -erint:

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | manducav**ero**, *I will have finished eating* | manducav**erimus** |
| 2. | manducav**eris** | manducav**eritis** |
| 3. | manducav**erit** | manducav**erint** |

Likewise: exercu**ero**, eg**ero**, rapu**ero**, finiv**ero** (or fini**ero**).

NOTE. — One will notice that eram is also the imperfect indicative of the verb esse, that ero is its future (but it makes erunt and not erint in the 3rd pers. pl.) and essem its imperfect subjunctive.

## 2. The passive conjugation

It is easily deduced from the preceding by very simple rules (cf. R. and N. 42, 4), with rare exceptions:

### 1° The series of the present

For the series of the present (infectum), it is enough to replace -o by -or (or -m by -r), -s by -ris, -t by -tur, -mus by -mur, -tis by -mini and -nt by -ntur.

E.g.: present passive indicative of manducare: manduc**or**, *I am being eaten*, manduc**aris**, manduc**atur**, manduc**amur**, manduc**amini**, manduc**antur**. Likewise: exerc**eor**, -eris, etc., rap**ior**, etc.

We will likewise have the present passive subjunctive: manduc**er**, manduc**eris**, etc.; exerc**ear**; rap**iar**; etc. and so on for the other tenses of the infectum.

As an exercise, try to find for yourself what the following correspond to: a) manducabatur; b) raperis; c) rapieris; d) manducaremini; e) manducabimur.

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

a) 3rd pers. sg. impf. ind.; b) 2nd pers. sg. pres. ind.; c) 2nd pers. sg. fut. ind.; d) 2nd pers. pl. impf. subj.; e) 1st pers. pl. fut. ind.

</details>

If you did not find raperis, that is quite normal, since the corresponding active form is rapis: you have just come across one of those exceptions we spoke of above. To go deeper into this question, refer to the grammatical appendix and compare the respective forms of each active conjugation and of its corresponding passive.

### 2° The series of the perfect

For the series of the perfect (perfectum) the rule is even simpler: it is enough to combine the perfect (passive) participle with an appropriate tense of the verb esse:

**a) Perfect indicative:**

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1. | manducatus sum, *I have been eaten* | manducati sumus |
| 2. | manducatus es | manducati estis |
| 3. | manducatus est | manducati sunt |

Pay attention to agreement in gender and number: *a woman has been eaten*, mulier manducat**a** est; *women*, …manducat**ae** sunt; *a thing* (neuter), manducat**um** est; *things*, manducat**a** sunt.

Likewise exercitus, actus, raptus, finitus… sum, es, etc.

*Perfect subjunctive*: sim, sis, etc., which is the present subjunctive of esse, is used: manducatus sim, *that I have been eaten*, manducatus sis, manducatus sit, manducati simus, sitis, sint. Likewise, exercitus sim, etc.

**b) Pluperfect indicative**: manducatus eram, *I had been eaten*, eras, etc., with the imperfect indicative of esse.

*Pluperfect subjunctive*: manducatus essem, *that I had been eaten*, esses, etc., with the imperfect subjunctive of esse.

**c) Future perfect indicative**: manducatus ero, *I will have been eaten*, eris, etc., with the future indicative of esse.

N.B. — In the personal tenses (indicative, subjunctive and imperative) deponent verbs are conjugated exactly like passive verbs.

## 3. The sequence of tenses

Let us simply take advantage of this overall view of the six tenses to say a few words about their use in the complex sentence. In sentences with several verbs, these are in principle put in the same tense, if the corresponding actions take place at the same time.

In the opposite case, one should remember that the tenses of the infectum and of the perfectum correspond two by two. Examples:

1. PRESENT: scio cur veneris, *I know why you have come* (ind. present and subj. perfect), that is to say PRESENT of the infectum and PRESENT of the perfectum.
2. PAST: sciebam cur venisses, *I knew why you had come* (ind. imperfect and subj. pluperfect), that is to say PAST of the infectum and PAST of the perfectum.
3. FUTURE: sciam cur veneris, *I will know why you have come* (ind. future and subj. perfect).

Of course other constructions are possible. For the moment simply know that tenses of the same name in Latin, even if one belongs to the infectum and the other to the perfectum, readily go together.

## 4. The conditional

This mood has no particular form in Latin, so it is replaced by the subjunctive and sometimes by the indicative. Simply note:

| | Latin | English | Mood and tense |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1° | possum si volo | *I can if I want* | simple supposition (indicative) |
| 2° | possim si velim | *I could if I wanted* (if, one day in the future, I came to want it) | *potential*: present subjunctive (present of the infectum) |
| 3° | possem si vellem | same translation as before, but implying: «in fact, at present, I do not want to» | *present unreal*: imperfect subjunctive (past of the infectum) |
| 4° | potuissem si voluissem | *I could have if I had wanted to* (but I did not want to) | *past unreal*: pluperfect subjunctive (past of the perfectum) |

The potential in fact corresponds to a situation that could, under certain conditions, come about in the future.

Phew! you will say at the end of this long revision. If you have held out until now, and if this last lesson has interested you, you can from now on consider yourself a full member of the Latin family!

If, on the contrary, you are having difficulties, do not despair: it is because the beneficial effect of repetition has not yet fully taken effect. Patience! Your perseverance will sooner or later be rewarded:

> Labor omnia vicit improbus, *work came out on top of everything [because it was] relentless.*

In any case, do not forget the 2nd wave. Today you should revise the 7th lesson.
